sense: take up a custom, a word, a way of doing things

terms.gloss: adopt, take up (rites, laws, customs, words); take in (a person as ally or citizen)
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.5.187: ā Graecīs adscīta et accepta
Hor. Ep. 2.2.119, of new words (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To take something over from others and make it one’s own, with thought or effort behind it (Lewis & Short): foreign rites, a law passed elsewhere, new words. Of persons, to receive someone as citizen, ally or son. The editions spell it both asc- and adsc-; quotations keep their edition’s spelling.

terms.gloss: adopt a plan, decide on a course
terms.grammar: phrase: cōnsilium capere + gen. of the gerund(ive), or ut + subjunctive
evidence: Caes. BG 3.2: legiōnis opprimendae cōnsilium capere (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Att. 7.10: subitō cōnsilium cēpī, ut exīrem (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: choose, take for oneself (a patron, a helper)
evidence: Cic. Div. Caec. 54: quem sibi illa dēfēnsōrem suī jūris adoptāvit (Lewis & Short, as Div. in Caecin. 16)
terms.comment: Its first sense, “take to oneself by choice”, used of persons; for an idea or a custom, ascīscere is the classical word. The common sense is to adopt a child (see adopt, a child).

phrases.latin: nē quid dīvīnī jūris neglegendō patriōs rītūs peregrīnōsque adscīscendō turbārētur
phrases.english: so that no part of divine law should be thrown into confusion by neglecting the native rites and adopting foreign ones

phrases.latin: quārum sacra populus Rōmānus ā Graecīs adscīta et accepta tantā religiōne et pūblicē et prīvātim tuētur
phrases.english: whose rites the Roman people took over from the Greeks and keep with such devotion, in public and in private

sources: Lewis & Short: ascisco · Lewis & Short: capio · Lewis & Short: adopto
